kids.text: Introduction and Terminology
Metallurgy: science of extraction of metals from ores in pure form
Mineral: naturally occurring chemical substance containing metal
Ore: mineral from which metal can be profitably extracted
Gangue: rocky, earthy, siliceous impurities associated with ore
Common ores: Bauxite (Al2O3.nH2O), Haematite (Fe2O3), Galena (PbS), Zinc blende (ZnS), Copper pyrite (CuFeS2)
Concentration of Ores
Removal of gangue to increase metal content; method depends on nature of ore and impurity
Gravity Separation (Hydraulic Wash)
Based on difference in specific gravity; ore heavier than gangue
Running water washes away lighter gangue particles
Used for native gold, haematite (Fe2O3), cassiterite (SnO2)
Froth Flotation
Used for sulphide ores (galena PbS, zinc blende ZnS)
Frothing agent: pine oil; Collector: sodium ethyl xanthate; Depressant: NaCN
Ore particles (oil-wetted) rise with froth; gangue settles at bottom
Leaching
Based on solubility of ore in suitable solvent; gangue remains insoluble
Cyanide leaching: gold ore + NaCN (aerated) → [Au(CN)2]- complex; recovered by Zn cementation
Alkali leaching: bauxite + NaOH at 470-520 K → soluble NaAlO2 (Bayer's process)
Magnetic Separation
Used when ore or impurity is magnetic; e.g., magnetite Fe3O4 separated from non-magnetic gangue
Extraction of Metals
Calcination: heating ore in limited air; drives off volatile matter (H2O, CO2); e.g., limestone → CaO
Roasting: heating sulphide ore in excess air; converts to oxide; SO2 is by-product
Smelting: heating ore with coke and flux in blast furnace; ore → metal + slag
Flux: substance combining with gangue to form fusible slag; CaO for SiO2 gangue (acidic-basic principle)
Thermodynamic Principles (Ellingham Diagram)
Ellingham diagram: plots Delta-G vs temperature for metal oxide formation; predicts feasibility of reduction
Metal with more negative Delta-G can reduce oxide of metal with less negative Delta-G
Carbon (coke) used as reducing agent above 983 K for most oxides; CO more effective below 983 K
Active metal oxides (Na, Al) not reducible by C; require electrolysis
Electrochemical Reduction
Delta-G = -nFE0; positive E0 means spontaneous reduction
Hall-Heroult process for Al: electrolysis of 20% Al2O3 in molten cryolite (Na3AlF6) at 1270 K
Cathode: pure Al deposited; Anode: carbon (consumed as CO2); cryolite lowers melting point
Refining Methods
Distillation: for volatile metals Zn (bp 1180 K) and Hg (bp 630 K)
Liquation: for low mp metals (Sn, Pb, Bi); crude metal heated on sloping hearth; pure metal flows
Electrolytic refining: crude metal = anode; pure metal = cathode; metal salt solution = electrolyte; anode mud has precious metals
Zone Refining
Based on fractional crystallisation; impurities more soluble in melt than solid
Induction heater moved along impure rod; impurities sweep to one end; used for Ge, Si, Ga
Vapour Phase Refining
Mond process (Ni): Ni + 4CO at 330 K → Ni(CO)4; decomposed at 460 K to pure Ni
Van Arkel method (Ti, Zr): impure metal + I2 at 550 K → TiI4; decomposed on W filament at 1800 K
Applications of Metals
Aluminium: cooking vessels, aircraft alloys (duralumin), overhead cables, foils, packaging
Zinc: galvanising iron (corrosion protection), die-casting, ZnO in paints and rubber
Iron/Steel: bridges, railways; stainless steel (Fe-Cr-Ni), nickel steel, chrome steel (cutting tools)
Copper: electrical wiring, bronze (Cu-Sn), brass (Cu-Zn), coins
General Trends in p-Block Elements
General configuration: ns2np1-6; Groups 13-18; includes metals, nonmetals and metalloids
Inert pair effect: heavier elements show (group OS - 2) stable state due to reluctance of ns2 electrons; e.g., Tl+ more stable than Tl3+
Anomalous behaviour of first element: small size, high IE, high EN, absence of d orbitals; diagonal relationship (B with Si)
Allotropism: many p-block elements exist in multiple forms; e.g., C: diamond, graphite, fullerene
Group 13 - Boron Family
Members: B, Al, Ga, In, Tl; configuration: ns2np1; most common OS: +3; Tl also shows +1 (inert pair)
Boron: metalloid; very high mp; forms covalent compounds; electron-deficient Lewis acid
Compounds of Boron
Borax (Na2B4O7.10H2O): gives bead test with metal oxides; used in glass and pottery glazes
Boric acid H3BO3: weak monobasic Lewis acid (accepts OH- from water); obtained from borax + HCl
Diborane B2H6: BF3 + LiAlH4 → B2H6; 3c-2e banana bonds; burns in air; hydrolysed by water
BF3: strong Lewis acid; forms adducts with Lewis bases (BF3.NH3); used as catalyst in organic reactions
Compounds of Aluminium
Al2O3: amphoteric oxide; reacts with both acid and base; alpha form (corundum) very hard
AlCl3: Lewis acid; catalyst in Friedel-Crafts; exists as dimer Al2Cl6 in vapour/non-aqueous media
Alum KAl(SO4)2.12H2O: double salt; water purification, dyeing, tanning, styptic agent
Group 14 - Carbon Family
Members: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb; configuration: ns2np2; highest OS: +4; Pb also shows +2 (inert pair)
Catenation: tendency to form chains; C >> Si > Ge >= Sn > Pb; C forms strongest C-C bonds
Allotropes of Carbon
Diamond: sp3 hybridised; 3D covalent network; hardest natural substance; non-conductor; used in cutting tools
Graphite: sp2 hybridised; layered structure; delocalised pi electrons; good conductor; used as lubricant, electrode
Fullerene C60 (Buckminsterfullerene): spherical cage; 20 hexagons + 12 pentagons; soccer ball shape
Graphene: single layer of graphite; sp2 C; strongest material; excellent conductor; 2D material
Carbon Monoxide (CO)
Preparation: incomplete combustion 2C + O2 → 2CO; lab: HCOOH + conc. H2SO4
Colourless, odourless, highly poisonous (binds Hb); strong reducing agent; forms metal carbonyls
Carbon Dioxide (CO2)
Linear molecule O=C=O; sp hybridised carbon; acidic oxide forms H2CO3 with water
Lime water test: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 (white ppt); excess CO2 → soluble Ca(HCO3)2
Silicon and its Compounds
SiO2 (silica): giant covalent 3D network of SiO4 tetrahedra; mp 1710°C; resists most acids except HF
Silicones: synthetic -Si-O-Si- backbone polymers; water-repellent, heat-stable; used in sealants and lubricants
Silicates: fundamental unit SiO4(4-) tetrahedron; ortho, pyro, chain, sheet, 3D network silicate structures
Group 15 - Nitrogen Family (Pnictogens)
Members: N, P, As, Sb, Bi; configuration: ns2np3; highest OS: +5; also +3 and -3
Nitrogen: diatomic N2; very inert due to N≡N bond (946 kJ/mol); 78% of atmosphere
Ammonia (NH3)
Haber's process: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3; Fe catalyst; 750 K, 200 atm; Le Chatelier: high P, moderate T
Lab: NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 on heating; collected by downward displacement of air (lighter than air)
Pyramidal shape; sp3 hybridised N; bond angle 107°; highly soluble in water; H-bonding
Basic: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-; forms ammonium salts with acids
Uses: manufacture of HNO3 (Ostwald process), fertilisers (urea, ammonium sulphate), refrigerant
Nitric Acid (HNO3)
Ostwald's process: NH3 + O2 (Pt, 800°C) → NO → NO2 + H2O → HNO3 (60-68%)
Strong oxidising agent; dissolves most metals; forms NO2 with conc., NO with dilute HNO3
Dilute HNO3 + Cu → Cu(NO3)2 + NO; conc. HNO3 + Cu → Cu(NO3)2 + NO2
Aqua regia: 1 part conc. HNO3 + 3 parts conc. HCl; dissolves Au and Pt
Passivation: Fe and Al resist conc. HNO3 due to protective oxide layer
Phosphorus and Compounds
Allotropes: white P4 (toxic, P4 tetrahedral), red (covalent polymer, less reactive), black (stable, graphite-like)
PCl3: trigonal pyramidal; sp3; hydrolysed by water → H3PO3 + 3HCl
PCl5: trigonal bipyramidal; sp3d; PCl3 + Cl2 → PCl5; dissociates at high temperature
Phosphoric acid H3PO4: tribasic (pKa1=2.1, pKa2=7.2, pKa3=12.4); used in fertilisers and soft drinks
Group 16 - Oxygen Family (Chalcogens)
Members: O, S, Se, Te, Po; configuration: ns2np4; OS: -2, +2, +4, +6
Oxygen: O2 (paramagnetic, diatomic); O3 (ozone, bent, diamagnetic); most electronegative after F
Ozone: strong oxidising agent; decomposes on warming; used for sterilisation, bleaching; protects UV rays
Allotropes of Sulphur
Rhombic sulphur (S8 rings, stable below 96°C, rhombic crystals, yellow) - most stable form
Monoclinic sulphur (above 96°C, needle-like crystals); plastic (amorphous, formed by quenching molten S)
Hydrogen Sulphide (H2S)
Preparation: FeS + dil. H2SO4 → H2S; bent molecule; weak dibasic acid
Reducing agent; precipitates metal sulphides used in qualitative analysis (group reagent)
Sulphuric Acid - Contact Process
Step 1: S + O2 → SO2; Step 2: 2SO2 + O2 (V2O5, 450-500°C) ⇌ 2SO3 (reversible)
Step 3: SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7 (oleum); Step 4: H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4
Properties: strong acid, oxidising agent, dehydrating agent, sulphonating agent
Hot conc. H2SO4 + C → CO2 + SO2; dissolves Cu, S, P; chars sugar/organic matter (dehydration)
Detection: BaCl2 solution gives white BaSO4 precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl
Uses: fertilisers (superphosphate), manufacture of HCl and HNO3, drying agent, explosives
Group 17 - Halogen Family
Members: F, Cl, Br, I, At; configuration: ns2np5; most reactive nonmetals; OS: -1 (F only), +1, +3, +5, +7
Reactivity: F > Cl > Br > I; electronegativity, oxidising power, bond dissociation energy decrease down the group
Chlorine
Lab: MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O; greenish-yellow, pungent gas
Industrial: electrolysis of brine (Chlor-alkali process); by-products: NaOH and H2
Strong oxidising and bleaching agent; bleaching permanent via nascent oxygen from Cl2 + H2O → HClO → [O]
Cl2 + cold dilute NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl (bleach); hot conc. NaOH → NaCl + NaClO3
Bleaching powder CaOCl2: Cl2 + Ca(OH)2; used in textile bleaching and water treatment
Hydrochloric Acid (HCl)
Lab: NaCl + conc. H2SO4 on gentle heating → NaHSO4 + HCl; strong monobasic acid
Aqua regia: 3 parts HCl + 1 part HNO3; dissolves noble metals Au and Pt by forming complexes
Interhalogen Compounds
Compounds of two different halogens: XY, XY3, XY5, XY7; more reactive than parent halogens
Examples: ClF (linear), BrF3 (T-shaped), IF5 (square pyramidal), IF7 (pentagonal bipyramidal)
Introduction
Transition elements: d-block; Groups 3-12; partially filled d orbitals in atom or common ion
General configuration: (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2; 3d (Sc-Zn), 4d (Y-Cd), 5d (La, Hf-Hg)
Zn, Cd, Hg excluded from typical TM (d10 in all OS); but included in d-block
General Characteristic Properties
Variable oxidation states: lose electrons from (n-1)d and ns orbitals; e.g., Mn: +2 to +7
Stability: half-filled (d5, Mn2+) and fully-filled (d10, Zn2+) configurations are extra stable
Metallic properties: high density, high mp/bp, high tensile strength; Cu and Ag are best conductors in 3d series
Small atomic/ionic radii due to poor shielding by d electrons; lanthanoid contraction: 4d ≈ 5d
Magnetic Properties
Paramagnetic: unpaired d electrons; magnetic moment mu = sqrt[n(n+2)] BM
Diamagnetic: all d electrons paired (e.g., Zn2+ d10; Sc3+ d0)
Ferromagnetic: Fe, Co, Ni; aligned domains; retain magnetism even without external field
Colour of Compounds
d-d electron transition absorbs visible light; complementary colour observed
Cu2+ (blue), Cr3+ (green), Mn2+ (faint pink), Fe3+ (yellow); d0 and d10 are colourless
Catalytic activity: variable OS and large surface area; Fe (Haber's), V2O5 (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt (Ostwald's)
Complex formation: small ionic size, high charge density; form stable coordination compounds with ligands
Alloy formation: similar atomic radii allow substitution; stainless steel, brass, bronze, nichrome
Important Compounds of d-Block
KMnO4: strong oxidising agent in acidic (MnO4- → Mn2+), alkaline (MnO4- → MnO2) and neutral media
K2Cr2O7: orange solid; from chromite ore; powerful oxidising agent in acidic medium
Dichromate-chromate interconversion: Cr2O7(2-) (acidic, orange) ⇌ CrO4(2-) (basic, yellow)
Standard electrode potentials: Cu has positive E0 (M2+/M); does not dissolve in dilute acids; Fe3+/Fe2+ = +0.77 V
Lanthanoids (4f series)
Ce (58) to Lu (71); configuration: [Xe] 4f1-14 5d0-1 6s2; mostly +3; Ce shows +4, Eu/Yb show +2
Lanthanoid contraction: steady decrease in ionic radii due to poor shielding by 4f electrons
Silvery white, reactive metals; react with water and acids; coloured ions; paramagnetic
Misch metal (alloy of La, Ce, Pr, Nd): used in lighter flints, alloy steels, catalytic converters
Actinoids (5f series)
Th (90) to Lr (103); configuration: [Rn] 5f1-14 6d0-1 7s2; all radioactive
Show variable OS (+3 to +7); more reactive than lanthanoids; actinoid contraction similar to lanthanoid
Th and U: naturally occurring; others are synthetic transuranic elements; Pu used in nuclear reactors
Introduction and Basic Terms
Coordination compound: central metal atom/ion bonded to ligands; Werner's theory (1893)
Ligand: ion or molecule donating electron pair to central metal; Lewis base
Coordination sphere: complex ion + counter ions; enclosed in square brackets
Coordination number: number of sigma-bonds between ligand donor atoms and central metal
Oxidation state: charge on central metal if all ligands removed with their electron pairs
Types of Ligands
Monodentate: one donor atom; e.g., Cl-, NH3, H2O, CN-, CO, OH-
Bidentate: two donor atoms; e.g., en (ethylenediamine), oxalate (C2O4(2-))
Polydentate: multiple donor atoms; EDTA is hexadentate (2N + 4O donors)
Ambidentate: can coordinate through more than one atom; NO2- (N or O); SCN- (S or N)
Chelate complex: polydentate ligands form ring with metal; more stable (chelate effect due to entropy)
IUPAC Nomenclature
Cation named first, then anion; ligands named alphabetically before central metal in complex
Anionic ligands end in 'o' (chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido); neutral: ammine, aqua, carbonyl, nitrosyl
Metal in anionic complex: Latin name + '-ate'; e.g., ferrate, cobaltate, plumbate, stannate
OS of central metal in Roman numerals in parentheses: [Fe(CN)6]4- = hexacyanidoferrate(II)
Multiplying prefixes: di/tri/tetra for simple; bis/tris/tetrakis for complex ligand names
Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
Structural Isomerism
Ionisation isomerism: [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 vs [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br; different anions inside/outside
Linkage isomerism: [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+ (N-bonded) vs [Co(NH3)5ONO]2+ (O-bonded); ambidentate ligand
Hydrate isomerism: [CrCl3(H2O)3] green vs [CrCl2(H2O)4]Cl blue-green vs [CrCl(H2O)5]Cl2 violet
Coordination isomerism: interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complex
Stereoisomerism
Geometrical: cis (same) vs trans (opposite); in square planar [MA2B2] and octahedral [MA2B4]
Facial (fac) vs meridional (mer) in octahedral [MA3B3]; fac: 3 identical at triangle vertices
Optical isomerism: non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers) in [M(en)3]n+; rotate polarised light
Bonding Theories
Valence Bond Theory (VBT)
Ligand lone pairs overlap with vacant hybrid orbitals of metal; coordinate covalent bond
Hybridisation and geometry: sp (linear), sp3 (tetrahedral), dsp2 (square planar), sp3d2/d2sp3 (octahedral)
Inner orbital (low spin, strong field): d2sp3; e.g., [Co(NH3)6]3+; outer orbital (high spin): sp3d2; e.g., [CoF6]3-
Limitations: cannot explain colour, spectrochemical series, or quantitative magnetic moments
Crystal Field Theory (CFT)
Ligands treated as point charges; electrostatic splitting of d orbitals in crystal field
Octahedral field: d orbitals split into t2g (lower: dxy, dyz, dxz) and eg (higher: dx2-y2, dz2); splitting = Delta-o
Tetrahedral field: Delta-t = 4/9 Delta-o; t2 above e; no square planar with weak field ligands normally
Spectrochemical series: I- < Br- < Cl- < F- < OH- < H2O < NH3 < en < CN- < CO (increasing field)
CFSE: Crystal Field Stabilisation Energy; high field → low spin (forced pairing); low field → high spin
Colour: d-d transition absorbs specific wavelength; complementary colour observed; [Ti(H2O)6]3+ is violet
Stability and Applications
Stability constant Kstab: higher Kstab → more stable; chelate effect increases stability
Biological complexes: haemoglobin (Fe-porphyrin), chlorophyll (Mg-porphyrin), Vitamin B12 (Co complex), carbonic anhydrase (Zn)
Applications: cis-platin [PtCl2(NH3)2] anticancer drug; EDTA removes heavy metal toxicity; electroplating; photography (AgCl + Na2S2O3)
Classification of Solids
Crystalline solids: long-range order; anisotropic; sharp melting point; true solids; e.g., NaCl, diamond, ice
Amorphous solids: short-range order; isotropic; no sharp mp; pseudo solids; e.g., glass, rubber, plastics
Types of crystalline solids
Ionic (NaCl, KCl): strong electrostatic forces; hard and brittle; high mp; conduct in molten/solution state
Covalent/network (diamond, SiO2): covalent 3D network; very hard; high mp; non-conductors generally
Molecular (ice, naphthalene): van der Waals/H-bonds; low mp; volatile; non-conductors
Metallic (Cu, Fe): metal cations in sea of electrons; good conductors; lustrous; malleable; ductile
Crystal Lattice and Unit Cell
Crystal lattice: 3D regular arrangement of constituent particles; lattice points
Unit cell: smallest repeating unit; parameters: edge lengths (a, b, c) and angles (alpha, beta, gamma)
7 crystal systems; 14 Bravais lattices (primitive, body-centred, face-centred, end-centred variations)
Cubic Unit Cells
Simple Cubic (SC)
Atoms at corners only; atoms per cell = 8 x 1/8 = 1; CN = 6; packing efficiency = 52.4%
Relation: a = 2r; example: polonium (only element with SC structure)
Body-Centred Cubic (BCC)
Atoms at corners + 1 body centre; atoms per cell = 2; CN = 8; packing efficiency = 68%
Relation: 4r = sqrt(3)a; examples: Na, K, W, Cr, Ba, Fe (at RT)
Face-Centred Cubic (FCC/CCP)
Atoms at corners + face centres; atoms per cell = 8x1/8 + 6x1/2 = 4; CN = 12; packing = 74%
Relation: 4r = sqrt(2)a; examples: Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Al; most efficient packing (ABCABC)
Close Packing and Voids
2D: square (less efficient) or hexagonal (more efficient) close packing
3D: ABAB = HCP (hexagonal); ABCABC = CCP/FCC (cubic); both have packing efficiency 74%
Tetrahedral void: CN = 4; number = 2N (for N atoms); smaller void
Octahedral void: CN = 6; number = N (for N atoms); larger void
Radius ratio r+/r-: determines crystal structure; 0.155-0.225 → tetrahedral; 0.414-0.732 → octahedral
X-Ray Diffraction and Density
Bragg's equation: 2d sin(theta) = n(lambda); determines interplanar spacing from X-ray data
Density: rho = nM/(Na x a^3); relates unit cell edge length to density; n = atoms per unit cell
Defects in Crystals
Stoichiometric Defects
Schottky defect: equal cations and anions missing; density decreases; in NaCl, KCl, KBr, CsCl
Frenkel defect: cation leaves lattice → interstitial site; density unchanged; in ZnS, AgBr, AgCl, AgI
Non-Stoichiometric Defects
Metal excess (F-centres): extra metal ions in interstitials; trapped electrons give colour; e.g., NaCl in Na vapour → yellow
Metal deficiency: fewer metal cations; e.g., FeO (Fe2+ replaced by Fe3+ to maintain electroneutrality)
Impurity defects: foreign atom substitutes host; e.g., SrCl2 in NaCl creates cation vacancy; doping in semiconductors
Electrical Properties
Conductors: overlapping bands or partially filled valence band; resistivity 10-6 to 10-8 ohm-m
Semiconductors: small band gap (~1 eV); conductivity increases with T; Si (1.1 eV), Ge (0.7 eV)
n-type: doping with Group 15 (donor) impurity; extra electrons as carriers; e.g., P in Si
p-type: doping with Group 13 (acceptor) impurity; holes as carriers; e.g., B in Si
Insulators: large band gap (>3 eV); no conduction at room temperature; e.g., diamond (5.4 eV)
Rate of Reaction
Rate: change in concentration per unit time; unit: mol/L/s; decreases with time
Rate = -(1/a)(d[A]/dt) = (1/b)(d[B]/dt) for aA → bB; stoichiometric coefficients normalise rate
Average rate: over a time interval; Instantaneous rate: tangent slope at a point on [C] vs t graph
Initial rate: at t = 0; used to determine rate law by method of initial rates
Rate Law and Rate Constant
Rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; k is rate constant; m, n determined experimentally (not from stoichiometry)
Overall order = m + n; units of k: (mol/L)^(1-n) s-1 for nth order
Zero order k: mol/L/s; First order k: s-1; Second order k: L/mol/s; pseudo-first order reactions
Integrated Rate Laws
Zero Order
Rate = k; [A] = [A]0 - kt; t1/2 = [A]0/2k; linear [A] vs t graph
Examples: photochemical decomposition of HI on gold; many enzyme-catalysed reactions at saturation
First Order
[A] = [A]0 e^(-kt); ln[A] = ln[A]0 - kt; linear ln[A] vs t graph with slope = -k
t1/2 = 0.693/k; independent of initial concentration; all radioactive decays are first order
Examples: decomposition of N2O5, H2O2; inversion of cane sugar; hydrogenation of ethylene
Second Order
1/[A] = 1/[A]0 + kt; linear 1/[A] vs t graph; t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0) depends on initial concentration
Examples: decomposition of NO2; saponification of ester in excess base
Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction
Nature of reactant: ionic reactions faster; bond breaking reactions slower; physical state matters
Concentration: rate increases with concentration; more frequent collisions; not for zero order
Temperature: rate roughly doubles per 10°C rise; temperature coefficient Q10 ≈ 2
Surface area: rate increases with surface area of solid reactant (powder vs lumps)
Catalyst: lowers activation energy; increases rate; not consumed; does not change equilibrium constant
Arrhenius Equation
k = A x e^(-Ea/RT); A = frequency/pre-exponential factor; Ea = activation energy
ln k = ln A - Ea/RT; plot ln k vs 1/T is linear; slope = -Ea/R; intercept = ln A
ln(k2/k1) = (Ea/R)(1/T1 - 1/T2); calculate Ea from k at two temperatures
Activation energy: minimum energy required for effective collision; lowered by catalyst
Collision Theory and Mechanism
Effective collision: energy >= Ea AND correct orientation (steric factor p)
Rate = Z x f x p; Z = collision frequency; f = e^(-Ea/RT) = fraction with sufficient energy
Transition state theory: reactants → activated complex (at energy maximum) → products; delta-G‡ determines rate
Rate-determining step: slowest elementary step in a multistep mechanism; governs overall rate
Theories of Acids and Bases
Arrhenius: acid → H+ in water; base → OH- in water; limitation: non-aqueous solvents, NH3
Bronsted-Lowry: acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor; conjugate acid-base pairs
Lewis: acid = electron pair acceptor; base = electron pair donor; broader concept; e.g., BF3 (Lewis acid)
Conjugate pairs: HA/A- and H2O/OH- (water as base); differ by one proton
Ionisation of Water and pH Scale
Autoionisation: H2O ⇌ H+ + OH-; Kw = [H+][OH-] = 10-14 at 25°C; increases with temperature
pH = -log[H+]; pOH = -log[OH-]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C; pH scale 0-14
Neutral: pH = 7; acidic: pH < 7; basic: pH > 7; strong acid pH = -log(Ca)
Weak Acids and Bases
Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA]; larger Ka → stronger acid; pKa = -log Ka
Ostwald's dilution law: alpha = sqrt(Ka/C); degree of dissociation increases on dilution
For weak acid: [H+] = sqrt(Ka x C); pH = (1/2)(pKa - log C)
Relative strength: Ka1/Ka2 = (alpha1/alpha2)^2 at same concentration
Common Ion Effect and Buffer Solutions
Common ion effect: adding common ion suppresses dissociation; shifts equilibrium left; reduces ionisation
Buffer: resists pH change on addition of small acid/base; consists of weak acid + its salt (acidic) or weak base + its salt (basic)
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); pOH = pKb + log([BH+]/[B])
Buffer capacity: maximum at pH = pKa; most effective when [acid] = [salt] ratio 1:1 to 10:1
Examples: blood (H2CO3/HCO3- buffer, pH ~7.4); acetate buffer (CH3COOH/CH3COONa)
Salt Hydrolysis
Strong acid + strong base (NaCl): no hydrolysis; pH = 7; Kh = Kw/(Ka x Kb)
Weak acid + strong base (CH3COONa): anion hydrolyses; pH > 7; pH = 7 + (1/2)(pKa - pKb)
Strong acid + weak base (NH4Cl): cation hydrolyses; pH < 7; pH = 7 - (1/2)(pKb)
Weak acid + weak base (CH3COONH4): pH = 7 + (1/2)(pKa - pKb)
Solubility Product (Ksp)
Ksp = [Am+]n[Bn-]m for AmBn ⇌ mAn+ + nBm-; derived from solubility (s)
If Q < Ksp: unsaturated; Q = Ksp: saturated; Q > Ksp: precipitate forms
Common ion effect: solubility decreases in presence of common ion; used in qualitative analysis
Selective precipitation: different Ksp values allow separation of ions by group reagents (H2S, NH3)
Conductance of Electrolytic Solutions
Conductance G = 1/R; unit: Siemens (S); specific conductance (kappa) = G x l/A
Molar conductance Lambda-m = kappa x 1000/M; increases with dilution (more ions)
Kohlrausch's law: Lambda(m,0) = lambda(+,0) + lambda(-,0); limiting molar conductance = sum of ionic conductances
For weak electrolytes: alpha = Lambda-m/Lambda-m(0); Ka = c*alpha^2/(1-alpha); conductance → Ka
Strong electrolytes: Lambda-m = Lambda-m(0) - b*sqrt(C) (Debye-Huckel-Onsager); linear plot
Galvanic (Voltaic) Cell
Converts chemical energy to electrical energy; spontaneous redox reaction; example: Daniel cell
Daniel cell: Zn|ZnSO4||CuSO4|Cu; E0cell = 1.1 V; Zn = anode (-), Cu = cathode (+)
Salt bridge: KCl or KNO3 in agar; maintains electrical neutrality; prevents mixing
E0cell = E0cathode - E0anode (both in reduction potential); positive E0 means spontaneous
Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE): reference electrode E0 = 0 V; H2 at 1 atm, 1 M H+, 298 K
Nernst Equation
E = E0 - (RT/nF)lnQ = E0 - (0.0591/n)logQ at 298 K; concentration dependence of cell potential
At equilibrium: E = 0 and Q = K; therefore E0 = (RT/nF)lnK; links thermodynamics to electrochemistry
Delta-G = -nFE; Delta-G0 = -nFE0 = -RT lnK; relates free energy to cell potential
Electrolysis and Faraday's Laws
Electrolytic cell: uses electrical energy for non-spontaneous redox; cathode (-), anode (+) - opposite to galvanic
Faraday's First Law: m = ZIt = (M/nF)It; mass deposited proportional to charge passed
Faraday's Second Law: same charge deposits masses proportional to equivalent masses (M/n)
1 Faraday = 96500 C = charge of 1 mole of electrons; moles of electrons = Q/F = It/F
Batteries and Fuel Cells
Primary Batteries (non-rechargeable)
Leclanche/dry cell: Zn anode; MnO2/C cathode; NH4Cl/ZnCl2 electrolyte; emf 1.5 V
Mercury button cell: Zn(amalgam)/HgO (+KOH); emf 1.35 V; pacemakers, watches, hearing aids
Secondary Batteries (rechargeable)
Lead storage battery: Pb(-)/H2SO4/PbO2(+); each cell 2V; 6 cells = 12 V; automobiles
Li-ion battery: graphite anode/CoO2 cathode/Li salt electrolyte; high energy density; phones, laptops
Nickel-cadmium cell: Cd anode/NiO(OH) cathode; 1.25 V per cell; power tools
Fuel cells: H2 + O2 → H2O + electricity; highly efficient (>70%); no pollution; used in space shuttles
Corrosion and Prevention
Electrochemical oxidation: Fe (anode) loses e- → Fe2+; O2 + H2O (cathode) → OH-; forms Fe(OH)2 → rust
Prevention: galvanising (Zn coat), painting, anodising (Al), sacrificial protection (Mg block near Fe), alloying
Adsorption
Adsorption: accumulation of substance on surface; adsorbent = surface; adsorbate = substance; exothermic
Types of Adsorption
Physisorption: weak van der Waals; delta-H 20-40 kJ/mol; reversible; multilayer; at low temperature
Chemisorption: chemical bond; delta-H 80-240 kJ/mol; irreversible; monolayer; at high temperature
Freundlich adsorption isotherm: x/m = kP^(1/n) at constant T; log(x/m) vs log P is linear
Factors: nature of adsorbent (surface area, pore structure), nature of adsorbate, temperature, pressure
Catalysis
Catalyst alters rate without permanent change; positive (increases rate) or negative (decreases rate, inhibitor)
Homogeneous catalysis: same phase; e.g., Cl- in H2O2 decomposition; NO in SO2 oxidation (lead chamber)
Heterogeneous (contact) catalysis: different phases; Fe in Haber's; V2O5 in Contact; Ni in hydrogenation
Enzyme catalysis
E + S → [ES complex] → E + P; highly specific (lock and key model); millions of molecules per minute
Optimum T ~37°C and optimum pH; denaturation above optimum temperature
Examples: zymase (glucose → ethanol + CO2), diastase (starch → maltose), urease (urea → NH3 + CO2)
Zeolites (shape-selective): microporous aluminosilicates; ZSM-5 used in petroleum refining (cracking)
Promoters: increase catalyst activity; Poisons: block active sites, decrease activity (e.g., As2O3 poisons Pt)
Colloids
Heterogeneous system; dispersed phase (1-1000 nm) in dispersion medium; intermediate between true solution and suspension
Types by phase
Sol (solid in liquid): Fe(OH)3 sol, ink, paint; Gel (liquid in solid): gelatin, cheese, butter
Emulsion (liquid in liquid): milk (O/W), cream (W/O), mayonnaise; Foam (gas in liquid): soap lather
Aerosol (liquid/solid in gas): fog/mist, clouds, smoke, dust
Preparation
Dispersion: mechanical (grinding), Bredig's arc (metals), peptisation (adding electrolyte to precipitate)
Condensation: double decomposition (As2S3 from H3AsO3 + H2S), reduction, oxidation, hydrolysis
Properties of Colloids
Tyndall effect: scattering of light; beam visible in colloidal solution; absent in true solutions
Brownian motion: random zigzag movement of colloidal particles; due to bombardment by solvent molecules
Electrophoresis: migration of charged colloidal particles under electric field; determines charge on colloid
Coagulation: aggregation and settling; Hardy-Schulze rule: higher valence of oppositely charged ion → more effective coagulation
Protective colloid: lyophilic colloid stabilises lyophobic colloid; gold number measures protective power
Applications
Water purification: alum coagulates negatively charged clay; Cottrell precipitator removes smoke
Cleansing action of soaps: micelle formation around grease; hydrophilic tail out, hydrophobic tail in
Delta formation: river colloidal particles coagulated by sea water electrolytes; medicines (colloidal drugs)
Alcohols
R-OH; 1° (primary), 2° (secondary), 3° (tertiary) based on carbon bearing -OH group
Preparation of Alcohols
Acid-catalysed hydration of alkenes: Markovnikov addition; oxymercuration-demercuration (anti-Markovnikov via hydroboration)
Reduction of carbonyl: NaBH4 (mild, RCHO → 1°, RCOR' → 2°); LiAlH4 (also reduces RCOOH → 1°)
Grignard: RMgX + HCHO → 1°; RCHO → 2°; RCOR' → 3° alcohol (after hydrolysis)
Fermentation: glucose → ethanol + CO2 (zymase enzyme); industrial production
Physical Properties
H-bonding: higher bp than alkanes/ethers of similar MW; miscibility with water decreases with chain length
Acidity: ROH + Na → RONa + H2; order: H2O > 1° > 2° > 3° (alkyl groups are EDG)
Chemical Properties
Lucas test: 3° fastest reaction with ZnCl2/conc. HCl (turbid immediately); 2° (5 min); 1° (no reaction)
Victor Meyer test: 1° → red; 2° → blue; 3° → colourless (with conc. H2SO4, KNO2, NH3, beta-naphthol)
Dehydration: at 170°C H2SO4 → alkene; at 130°C → ether (intermolecular); follows Saytzeff's rule
Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde (PCC) → carboxylic acid (KMnO4); 2° → ketone; 3° → oxidative cleavage
Esterification: ROH + RCOOH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O; acid-catalysed, reversible; Fischer esterification
Phenols
Ar-OH; more acidic than alcohols (pKa ~10) due to resonance stabilisation of phenoxide ion
Preparation: cumene process (commercial); diazonium salt hydrolysis; from chlorobenzene (NaOH, 300 atm)
Reactions of Phenols
EAS: -OH strongly o-/p-directing and activating; bromination (Br2 water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol)
Kolbe-Schmitt: Na-phenoxide + CO2 (150°C, 4-7 atm) → salicylic acid (o-hydroxybenzoic acid)
Reimer-Tiemann: phenol + CHCl3/NaOH → o-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde)
FeCl3 test: phenol → violet colour (ferric complex); distinguishes phenol from alcohol
Ethers
R-O-R'; IUPAC: shorter alkyl group as alkoxy prefix; e.g., CH3OC2H5 = methoxyethane
Preparation
Williamson synthesis: R-ONa + R'X → R-O-R' + NaX; SN2 mechanism; best for unsymmetrical ethers
Intermolecular dehydration: ROH + H2SO4 at 413 K → ROR (only symmetrical ethers efficiently)
Chemical Properties
Cleavage with HI (strongest) > HBr > HCl; SN2 on smaller alkyl group
Autooxidation in air forms explosive peroxides; store with metal wire/reducing agent
Anisole EAS: -OCH3 is o-/p-directing; Friedel-Crafts, nitration, halogenation possible
Uses: diethyl ether as anaesthetic and solvent; crown ethers as complexing agents; dioxane as solvent
Aldehydes and Ketones - Introduction
Aldehydes (-CHO): R-CHO; ketones: R-CO-R'; carbonyl C is sp2 hybridised; C=O bond polar (C delta+, O delta-)
IUPAC: suffix '-al' for aldehyde; '-one' with position for ketone; aldehyde C is always C-1
Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones
Oxidation of alcohols: 1° alcohol + PCC → aldehyde; 2° alcohol + KMnO4 → ketone
Rosenmund reduction: RCOCl + H2 (Pd-BaSO4, quinoline) → RCHO (selective, stops at aldehyde)
Stephen's reduction: RCN + SnCl2/HCl → imine salt → hydrolysis → RCHO
Etard reaction: ArCH3 + CrO2Cl2 → Etard complex → water → ArCHO (e.g., toluene → benzaldehyde)
Gattermann-Koch: ArH + CO + HCl (AlCl3, CuCl) → ArCHO (aromatic aldehydes)
Ozonolysis of alkenes: alkene + O3 → ozonide → Zn/H2O → carbonyl compounds
Friedel-Crafts acylation: ArH + RCOCl (AlCl3) → Ar-CO-R (ketone)
Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
Nucleophilic addition mechanism: Nu:- attacks electrophilic C of C=O → tetrahedral intermediate → product
With HCN → cyanohydrin (RCHOHCN); with NaHSO3 → bisulphite adduct (crystalline, used for ID and separation)
With alcohols: RCHO + ROH (dry HCl) → hemiacetal → acetal; reversible; ketones form hemiketal → ketal
With NH2 derivatives
With NH2OH → oxime; NH2NH2 → hydrazone; NH2NHC6H5 → phenylhydrazone; NH2NHCONH2 → semicarbazone
All follow condensation mechanism; loss of H2O; products used for characterisation
Reduction: NaBH4/LiAlH4 → alcohol; Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/conc. HCl) → hydrocarbon; Wolff-Kishner (NH2NH2/KOH/heat) → hydrocarbon
Aldol Condensation
Carbonyl with alpha-H + dilute NaOH → beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound (aldol product)
On heating: dehydration → alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl; crossed aldol gives mixed products
Cannizzaro Reaction (no alpha-H aldehyde)
HCHO/C6H5CHO + conc. NaOH → simultaneous oxidation (acid/salt) and reduction (alcohol)
C6H5CHO → C6H5CH2OH + C6H5COONa; HCHO → CH3OH + HCOONa
Perkin reaction: ArCHO + (RCO)2O + RCOONa → ArCH=CRCOOH (e.g., benzaldehyde → cinnamic acid)
Tests for Aldehydes
Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO3): aldehyde → silver mirror; ketones fail; aromatic + aliphatic both react
Fehling's solution: aliphatic aldehydes → red Cu2O precipitate; aromatic aldehydes and ketones fail
Schiff's reagent (rosaniline + SO2): aldehyde → pink/red; ketones fail (except formaldehyde reversal)
Iodoform test (CHI3 yellow ppt): CH3CHO and CH3COR and CH3CH(OH) compounds give positive test
Carboxylic Acids
-COOH group; sp2 C; resonance hybrid; acidic (pKa ~4-5); stronger than phenols and alcohols
Preparation
Oxidation: 1° alcohol or aldehyde + KMnO4/K2Cr2O7 → RCOOH; ArCH3 → ArCOOH
Hydrolysis of nitriles: RCN + H2O (H+ or OH-) → RCOOH + NH3
Grignard: RMgX + CO2 (dry) → RCOOMgX → (H3O+) → RCOOH; carbon chain extended by 1
Chemical Properties
Acidic nature: RCOOH ⇌ RCOO- + H+; EWG substituents increase acidity; EDG decrease acidity
Esterification: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H2O; acid-catalysed; Fischer esterification
Reactions: → RCOCl (SOCl2); → (RCO)2O (P2O5); → RCONH2 (NH3 then heat); → RCOOH + Br2 (HVZ reaction for alpha-bromo acid)
Decarboxylation: RCOOH + NaOH (CaO) → RH + Na2CO3 (Duma's reaction for lower acids)
Acidity trends: HCOOH > CH3COOH > C2H5COOH; Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH
Nitro Compounds
R-NO2 (nitroalkanes) and Ar-NO2 (nitroarenes); classified as primary, secondary, tertiary based on carbon type
Tautomerism: 1° and 2° nitroalkanes show nitro ⇌ aci-nitro equilibrium (involving alpha-H)
Acidic character: NO2 is EWG; alpha-H acidic; dissolve in NaOH; more acidic than aldehydes
Preparation
From alkyl halides: R-X + AgNO2 → R-NO2 (major) + R-O-N=O (alkyl nitrite, minor)
Vapour phase nitration of alkanes: RH + HNO3 (400°C) → mixture of nitroalkanes
Nitration of arenes: ArH + conc. HNO3 + H2SO4 → ArNO2; -NO2 is meta-directing for further substitution
Reduction of nitrobenzene
Strongly acidic (Sn/HCl): C6H5NO2 → aniline (C6H5NH2)
Neutral (Zn/NH4Cl): → N-phenylhydroxylamine (C6H5NHOH)
Alkaline medium: Zn/NaOH → azoxybenzene; LiAlH4 → azobenzene; Zn/NaOH (excess) → hydrazobenzene
Amines
Organic derivatives of NH3; 1° (RNH2), 2° (R2NH), 3° (R3N); aliphatic and aromatic
Preparation
Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: phthalimide + KOH + RX → N-alkylphthalimide + N2H4 → primary amine only
Hoffmann bromamide degradation: RCONH2 + Br2 + KOH → RNH2 (one carbon less); rearrangement
Reduction: RCN + LiAlH4 → RCH2NH2; RCONH2 + LiAlH4 → RCH2NH2; RNO2 + H2 (Raney Ni) → RNH2
Ammonolysis of alkyl halide: R-X + excess NH3 → RNH2 + R2NH + R3N + R4N+X- (mixture)
Basicity of Amines
Lone pair on N donates to H+; alkyl groups (+I effect) increase electron density on N; base strength increases
Aqueous basicity order: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 (due to solvation effect of water on ammonium ion)
Gas phase basicity: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3 (inductive effect only; no solvation)
Aniline (pKb 9.4) much less basic: lone pair delocalised into benzene ring; not freely available
Identification Tests
Carbylamine test (isocyanide): 1° amine + CHCl3 + KOH → isocyanide (foul smell); unique to primary amines
Hinsberg test: C6H5SO2Cl; 1° → sulphonamide soluble in KOH; 2° → insoluble; 3° → no reaction
HNO2 (NaNO2/HCl at 0-5°C): 1° → diazonium salt (stable Ar, unstable aliphatic); 2° → N-nitroso oil; 3° → no reaction
Chemical Properties
Acetylation: RNH2 + (CH3CO)2O → RNHCOCH3 + CH3COOH; protects -NH2 in organic synthesis
EAS on aniline: -NH2 strongly ortho-/para-directing and activating; but in acidic medium -NH3+ is meta-directing
Sandmeyer reaction via diazonium: ArNH2 → ArN2+ → ArCl/Br/CN/F/OH depending on reagent
Diazonium Salts
Diazotisation: ArNH2 + NaNO2 + HCl (0-5°C) → ArN2+Cl- (diazonium salt); aromatic more stable than aliphatic
Reactions of Diazonium Salts
Sandmeyer: ArN2+ + CuX → ArX + N2 (X = Cl, Br, CN using Cu2Cl2, Cu2Br2, CuCN respectively)
Gattermann: ArN2+ + Cu + HX → ArX; Balz-Schiemann: ArN2+BF4- → ArF + N2 + BF3 (to introduce F)
Coupling reaction: ArN2+ + phenol/amine (at p position) → azo dye (-N=N- chromophore); EAS on coupling component
Gomberg reaction: ArN2+ + NaOH + benzene → biaryl (Ar-Ar'); free radical mechanism
Carbohydrates
Polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones Cn(H2O)n; photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2
Classification: monosaccharides (cannot hydrolyse); oligosaccharides (2-10 units); polysaccharides (>10 units)
Monosaccharides
Glucose (C6H12O6): aldohexose; 5 -OH and 1 -CHO; open chain (Fischer) and ring form (Haworth/glucopyranose)
Fructose: ketohexose; sweeter than glucose; C2 is ketone carbon; found in fruits and honey
D/L configuration: penultimate C -OH position; D = right (natural form); L = left (synthetic)
Alpha and beta anomers: differ at anomeric carbon (C1 of aldoses); mutarotation in solution between alpha and beta
Disaccharides
Sucrose: alpha-D-glucose + beta-D-fructose (alpha1-beta2 glycosidic bond); non-reducing sugar; inversion by sucrase
Maltose: two alpha-D-glucose units (alpha1-4 glycosidic bond); reducing sugar; from starch hydrolysis
Lactose: galactose + glucose (beta1-4); reducing sugar; in milk; lactose intolerance due to lack of lactase
Polysaccharides
Starch: amylose (linear alpha1-4 bonds, helix) + amylopectin (branched alpha1-4 and alpha1-6); energy storage in plants
Glycogen: animal starch; more branched than amylopectin; stored in liver and muscles
Cellulose: beta1-4 glucose; structural (plant cell walls); not hydrolysed by human enzymes; dietary fibre
Reducing sugars: free aldehyde or ketone group; reduce Tollens/Fehling; all monosaccharides; sucrose = non-reducing
Osazones: monosaccharides + phenylhydrazine → yellow crystalline osazones; used for identification and characterisation
Proteins and Amino Acids
Amino acids: -NH2 (at alpha-C) and -COOH; 20 natural L-amino acids; zwitterion form at isoelectric point
Peptide bond: -CO-NH- formed by condensation between -COOH and -NH2; primary structure of protein
Protein Structure Levels
Primary: amino acid sequence linked by peptide bonds; determines all higher structures
Secondary: alpha-helix (H-bonds within chain, 3.6 residues/turn) or beta-pleated sheet (H-bonds between chains)
Tertiary: 3D folding; stabilised by H-bonds, disulphide bridges (-S-S-), hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic forces
Quaternary: association of 2+ polypeptide subunits; e.g., haemoglobin (4 subunits: 2 alpha + 2 beta)
Classification of Proteins
Simple proteins: amino acids only; albumin, globulin, keratin (hair/nails), collagen (connective tissue)
Conjugated proteins: protein + prosthetic group; glycoprotein, lipoprotein, nucleoprotein, haemoglobin (chromoprotein)
Denaturation: disruption of 2°/3°/4° structure by heat, pH, organic solvents; protein loses biological activity; 1° intact
Enzymes
Biological catalysts; complex proteins; lock and key model (substrate fits active site); highly specific
E + S → [ES complex] → E + P; rate maximum at optimum pH and temperature; inhibited by poisons
Cofactors: coenzymes (organic: NAD, FAD, coenzyme A) or metal ions (Zn2+ in carbonic anhydrase, Mg2+ in hexokinase)
Examples: amylase (starch → maltose), pepsin (proteins in stomach), lipase (fats → fatty acids), urease (urea → NH3 + CO2)
Nucleic Acids
Polynucleotides; nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate; linked by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds
DNA: deoxyribose; A, T, G, C bases; double helix (Watson-Crick, 1953); A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds)
RNA: ribose; A, U, G, C bases; single-stranded; mRNA (template), tRNA (anticodon), rRNA (ribosome component)
Central dogma: DNA → RNA (transcription) → protein (translation); DNA replication is semi-conservative
Vitamins, Lipids and Hormones
Fat-soluble vitamins: A (retinol, night blindness), D (calciferol, rickets), E (tocopherol, fertility), K (clotting)
Water-soluble vitamins: B1 (thiamine, beri-beri), B2 (riboflavin), B12 (pernicious anaemia), C (ascorbic acid, scurvy)
Lipids: fats = glycerol + saturated fatty acids (solid); oils = glycerol + unsaturated fatty acids (liquid); energy storage
Hormones: chemical messengers from endocrine glands; insulin (blood glucose), adrenaline (fight/flight), thyroxine (metabolism)
Drugs and Medicines
Drug: modifies physiological systems; therapeutic index = max tolerated dose / min curative dose; higher = safer
Classification of drugs
By chemical structure: penicillins (similar skeleton), opiates, steroids, barbiturates
By pharmacological effect: antibiotics, analgesics, antihypertensives, antihistamines
By molecular target: enzyme inhibitors, receptor agonists/antagonists, nucleic acid binders
Drug-Target Interaction
Competitive enzyme inhibitor: same active site as substrate; e.g., sulphanilamide mimics PABA → inhibits DHPS in bacteria
Allosteric inhibitor: binds at site other than active site; changes active site geometry; substrate cannot bind
Receptor agonist: mimics natural messenger; activates receptor; e.g., morphine (pain relief)
Receptor antagonist: blocks receptor without activating it; e.g., caffeine (blocks adenosine receptor → wakefulness)
Classes of Drugs
Tranquilizers: act on CNS; block dopamine; treat anxiety, depression, schizophrenia; e.g., diazepam (Valium), haloperidol, alprazolam
Non-narcotic analgesics: aspirin (NSAID, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, antiplatelet), paracetamol, ibuprofen
Narcotic analgesics (opioids): morphine, codeine; severe pain relief; addictive; can cause coma in overdose
Antibiotics: amoxicillin, ampicillin, tetracycline, erythromycin; kill or inhibit bacteria; broad/narrow spectrum
Sulfa drugs: sulphanilamide; competitive inhibitor of DHPS; bacteriostatic; oldest chemotherapeutic agent
Antacids: Mg(OH)2, Al(OH)3 neutralise HCl; cimetidine/ranitidine block H2 receptors (structurally similar to histamine)
Antihistamines: brompheniramine, terfenadine; block histamine H1 receptors; treat allergies, hay fever
Antiseptics: on living tissue; boric acid (eyes), iodoform, dettol (chloroxylenol + terpineol), phenol (<1%)
Disinfectants: on non-living surfaces; phenol (>1%), bleaching powder, SO2, ethylene oxide; more toxic than antiseptics
Antifertility drugs: synthetic oestrogen (ethinylestradiol) + progesterone (norethindrone); oral contraceptives
Food Additives
Artificial sweeteners: saccharin (550x), aspartame (100x, unstable above 200°C), sucralose (600x, from sucrose), alitame (2000x)
Food preservatives: sodium benzoate, potassium sorbate, sugar, salt, vinegar (acetic acid); prevent microbial growth
Antioxidants: BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole), BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene); prevent rancidity of fats in food
Nutritional additives: vitamins, minerals, amino acids added to fortify food (e.g., iodised salt, vitamin-fortified milk)
Cleansing Agents
Soaps
RCOONa; saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol; hard soap (NaOH), soft soap (KOH), transparent (alcohol)
Cleansing: micelle formation; hydrophobic tail inside (grease), hydrophilic head outside (water)
Limitation: precipitate with hard water Ca2+/Mg2+ → scum; ineffective in sea water and acidic water
Synthetic Detergents
Anionic: sodium lauryl sulphate CH3(CH2)11OSO3Na; sodium dodecylbenzenesulphonate; used in most household detergents
Cationic: quaternary ammonium salts (cetyltrimethylammonium bromide); also germicidal; used in disinfectants, fabric softeners
Non-ionic: polyethylene glycol esters; non-foaming; effective in hard water; used in dishwashers
Advantage over soaps: work in hard, soft and acidic water; biodegradable (linear) vs non-biodegradable (branched)
Polymers
High molecular mass molecules from monomers; degree of polymerisation = n; addition or condensation type
Types of Polymerisation
Addition (chain-growth): monomers add to chain; no by-product; needs C=C double bond; free radical, cationic or anionic mechanism
Condensation (step-growth): bifunctional monomers react with loss of small molecule (H2O, HCl); builds up gradually
Copolymerisation: two or more monomers polymerise together; e.g., Buna-S, ABS (acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene)
Structure Types
Linear: long straight chains; high density; strong; e.g., HDPE, nylon-6,6, PET
Branched: side chains on main chain; lower density, lower mp; e.g., LDPE, amylopectin
Cross-linked (network): 3D covalent network; hard, rigid, thermosetting; e.g., Bakelite, melamine-formaldehyde, vulcanised rubber
Important Polymers
Nylon-6,6: hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid; strong, elastic; fabrics, ropes, gears, stockings
Terylene/Dacron: ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid; polyester; wrinkle-resistant; bottles, fabrics, films
Bakelite: phenol + formaldehyde; thermosetting; electrical insulator; switches, handles, billiard balls
Natural rubber: cis-1,4-polyisoprene; vulcanisation with S (cross-links) → elastic, strong; tyres, gloves
Neoprene: poly(2-chloro-1,3-butadiene); oil-resistant; wetsuits, cables, gaskets
Buna-S (SBR): styrene + butadiene; most widely used synthetic rubber; car tyres
PHBV: poly(beta-hydroxybutyrate-co-beta-hydroxyvalerate); biodegradable; medical implants, packaging, controlled drug release
Teflon (PTFE): tetrafluoroethylene polymer; non-stick cookware, bearings, gaskets; extremely chemically inert
